issues.legal_issue: An abatement may be set aside despite delay and negligence where the appeal concerns a preliminary partition decree, the deceased party’s heirs sought to be joined, and hearing the appeal on its merits would not cause irreparable prejudice.
material_facts: The proceeding was an appeal from a preliminary decree in a partition suit.
The deceased respondent was a near relation of the appellants, and the appellants knew of the death but did not apply to substitute the legal representatives within time.
The deceased respondent’s heirs applied to be brought on record, although they relied on an inappropriate procedural route.
In a partition suit, parties may change between plaintiff and defendant, and the preliminary decree had declared their shares.
The Court considered that hearing the appeal on its merits would not cause irreparable prejudice, although it would prolong the partition proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court’s refusal to set aside the abatement and bring the legal representatives on record, and directed that the appeal be heard on its merits.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order 22 Rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the legal representatives of a deceased party must be brought on record when the cause survives; otherwise, the proceeding abates, subject to the power to set aside abatement for sufficient cause. Order 1 Rule 10 is a general joinder provision and ordinarily is not a substitute for the specific procedure in Order 22 Rule 4. Procedural rules facilitate justice but must be obeyed; courts may excuse a lapse in an appropriate case, but not as a matter of course. Negligence or laches ordinarily do not justify setting aside abatement, though the overall circumstances may warrant relief in a rare case. The Court relied on Sangram Singh v. Election Tribunal, Kotah and Kalipar Das v. Bimal Krishna Sen for the purpose of procedural law, and treated the nature of a partition proceeding and the absence of irreparable prejudice as material in this case.

rule.if: appeal_from_preliminary_partition_decree and appellants_knew_of_death and substitution_was_delayed and deceased_party_heirs_sought_to_join_record and parties_could_change_roles_in_partition and merits_hearing_would_not_cause_irreparable_prejudice

predicates.appeal_from_preliminary_partition_decree: The proceeding was an appeal from a preliminary decree in a partition suit.
predicates.appellants_knew_of_death: The appellants knew that a respondent had died.
predicates.substitution_was_delayed: The appellants did not seek substitution within the required time and were negligent in doing so.
predicates.deceased_party_heirs_sought_to_join_reco: The deceased party’s heirs applied to be brought into the proceeding, though their application used an inappropriate procedural route.
predicates.parties_could_change_roles_in_partition: The nature of the partition proceeding allowed parties to change between plaintiff and defendant.
predicates.merits_hearing_would_not_cause_irreparab: The Court considered that deciding the appeal on its merits would not cause irreparable prejudice to the parties.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a preliminary partition decree involves delayed substitution, an attempt by the deceased party’s heirs to join the proceeding, parties who can change roles, and no irreparable prejudice from a merits hearing, the abatement is set aside and the appeal proceeds on its merits.
